- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the introduction to a guide for a REST API that manages calendar bookings. Around 200 words.

# Bookings API

This API manages calendar bookings: creating them, moving them, cancelling them, and answering the question of when a resource is free.

A booking is a block of time attached to a resource — a room, a person, a piece of equipment — plus whatever metadata your application needs to hang on it. Resources declare their own availability windows. The API refuses any booking that falls outside those windows or collides with an existing one, so double-booking is a 409 rather than a problem you discover later.

Everything speaks JSON over HTTPS. Authentication is a bearer token in the `Authorization` header; tokens are scoped per workspace, and a token can only see resources in its own workspace. All timestamps go over the wire as RFC 3339 with an explicit offset. Resources store an IANA timezone name, which is what the API uses when it decides whether 09:00 on a Tuesday falls inside business hours.

Reads are cheap and paginated with opaque cursors. Writes accept an `Idempotency-Key` header, which matters more than it sounds like it does: a booking request that times out mid-flight can be safely retried without creating a duplicate.

The sections that follow cover authentication, the resource and booking objects, availability queries, recurrence, and webhooks. If you want to see a booking created end to end before reading any of that, start with the quickstart.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a paragraph on authentication.

Every request carries a bearer token in the `Authorization` header: `Authorization: Bearer sk_live_...`. Tokens are issued per workspace from the dashboard and do not expire on a timer; you revoke them explicitly, and revocation takes effect on the next request. A missing or malformed header returns 401. A token that is well-formed but scoped to a different workspace returns 404 rather than 403, so a caller cannot use error codes to learn which booking IDs exist elsewhere. Each token also carries a scope list (`bookings:read`, `bookings:write`, `resources:write`), and a call outside those scopes returns 403 with the missing scope named in the body. These tokens are for server-side use. Do not ship one to a browser or a mobile app; use the short-lived session tokens covered under client access.

# Authentication

To use this API, your program has to prove who it is on every single request. It does that by sending a token — a long secret string that looks like `sk_live_...` — along with each request, in a part of the request called a header:

```
Authorization: Bearer sk_live_abc123...
```

You get a token from the dashboard. It belongs to one workspace, and it keeps working until you go back to the dashboard and revoke it; there is no expiry date to track. Once revoked, the very next request with it fails.

If you forget the header, or type it wrong, the API answers with status code 401, which means "I don't know who you are." If you use a real token but ask for a booking that belongs to somebody else's workspace, you get 404, the same code you get for a booking that doesn't exist at all. That is deliberate: it stops a stranger from probing the API to find out which booking IDs are real.

A token also has a list of permissions attached, such as `bookings:read` or `bookings:write`. Try something the token has no permission for, and the API returns 403 and names the permission you are missing.

One rule to take seriously: keep the token on your own server. Never put it in a web page or a phone app, because anyone can read it there and then act as you. For those, see the client access section.
